teaser: Loops, whorls, and arches are only the beginning of the pattern.
title: Fingerprints
question: How can fingertips share three big patterns yet keep different tiny details?
idea: Raised friction ridges can flow in loops, whorls, or arches, while tiny ridge endings and splits make each print more detailed.

curiosity.intro: A faint mark, a magnifier, and a map hidden on every fingertip.
curiosity.carryForward: Follow the ridges from the big flow to the tiniest fork.

questions.question: What made the curved lines on the glass?
questions.notice: Look for the pale ridges and the darker spaces between them.
questions.say: A fingertip has raised lines called friction ridges, with lower grooves between them. When ridge tops touch a surface, sweat and natural skin oils can leave a faint impression of their paths.
questions.try: Tilt a clean drinking glass toward a lamp and look for a faint print. Keep the glass on the table while you look.

questions.question: Which way do the ridges flow?
questions.notice: Trace one curve in each large pattern card with your eyes.
questions.say: Many fingerprints can be grouped by their broad ridge flow. A loop curves back toward one side, a whorl circles around a center, and an arch rises and crosses from one side to the other.
questions.try: Draw one loop, one circle-like whorl, and one hill-shaped arch on paper.

questions.question: Can two loops still be different?
questions.notice: Find a ridge that ends and another that splits into two paths.
questions.say: The big pattern family is only a first clue. Along the ridges are smaller details: a line may end, split, shorten, or bend. Two prints can both be loops while their tiny details appear in different places.
questions.try: On two drawn loops, add endings and forks in different places. Compare your maps.

questions.question: Why does a print have dark lines and pale gaps?
questions.notice: Compare the inked fingertip with the print it leaves on paper.
questions.say: Washable ink touches the raised ridge tops. When the fingertip presses paper, those tops transfer dark lines while the lower grooves leave pale spaces. The print is a flat impression of a textured fingertip.
questions.try: Use a non-toxic washable stamp pad on one fingertip, press once on paper, and wash your hands. Keep the paper at home.

reading.title: The map on a fingertip
reading.coverText: A faint mark becomes a map of ridges, curves, endings, and splits.
reading.foldableTitle: A little book of ridge maps
reading.foldableNote: Follow one faint mark from its broad flow to its tiniest details.
reading.parentNote: Age 8. Welcome pointing, speech, drawing, or dictation. Keep any paper prints at home and do not upload or share them.

beats.title: A mark on the glass
beats.passage: Morning light crossed the table, and a faint swirl appeared on a drinking glass. Little Wonderer tilted the magnifier. The mark was not one solid smudge. It held many curved lines. Big wondered aloud, “What part of a fingertip could leave a map like that?”
beats.prompt: What first showed that the mark held a pattern?

foldable.heading: A mark on the glass
foldable.body: Morning light revealed a faint swirl on a glass. Under the magnifier, Little saw many curved lines instead of one plain smudge.

beats.title: Ridges and grooves
beats.passage: A close look at a fingertip revealed raised lines with lower spaces between them. The raised lines were friction ridges; the lower spaces were grooves. Only the ridge tops had touched the glass, leaving a flat impression of the fingertip's textured surface.
beats.prompt: Why did the impression show separate lines instead of one dark patch?

foldable.heading: Ridges and grooves
foldable.body: A fingertip has raised friction ridges and lower grooves. The ridge tops touched the glass and left separate curved lines.

beats.title: Three broad flows
beats.passage: Big placed three field cards on the table. One pattern curved back toward the side: a loop. One circled a center: a whorl. One rose like a hill and crossed the card: an arch. These families described the broad flow, but they did not tell the whole story.
beats.prompt: How does an arch's flow differ from a loop's flow?

foldable.heading: Three broad flows
foldable.body: Loops curve back, whorls circle a center, and arches rise across. These families describe the broad flow, not every tiny detail.

beats.title: Look inside the loop
beats.passage: Two cards both held loops. At first they seemed alike. Then Little found a ridge that ended on one card and continued on the other. Another ridge split into two paths at a different place. The tiny endings and splits turned each broad loop into a more detailed map.
beats.prompt: Which evidence showed that the two loops were not the same map?

foldable.heading: Inside the loop
foldable.body: Two prints were both loops, yet their small details differed. Ridges ended and split in different places across each map.

beats.title: A print on paper
beats.passage: Little touched one fingertip to a washable stamp pad, then pressed paper once. Ink rode on the raised ridge tops. The lower grooves stayed pale. The paper held an impression: dark ridge paths with light spaces between them. After one careful look, the print stayed at home and hands were washed.
beats.prompt: Which parts of the fingertip carried ink to the paper?

foldable.heading: A print on paper
foldable.body: Washable ink coated the raised ridge tops. They made dark paths on paper while the lower grooves left pale spaces.

beats.title: Same map, new mark
beats.passage: A second press looked lighter and a little smudged, but the same turns, endings, and splits still lined up. Pressure had changed the impression's clarity, not the ridge map beneath it. Little set a different fingertip print beside the pair. Its broad flow and tiny details made a new map to explore.
beats.prompt: How could Little tell that the lighter print came from the same ridge map?

foldable.heading: Same map, new mark
foldable.body: A lighter press looked smudged, but its turns, endings, and splits still lined up. Pressure changed the mark, not the ridge map.

yourTurn.title: Your turn
yourTurn.prompt: Write a compare sentence about two ridge maps.
yourTurn.example: Example: Both prints are loops, but this ridge ends sooner.

math.title: Number crunch at the print table
math.intro: Regroup tens and ones while you count paper ridge marks, cards, and magnifiers.

tasks.prompt: Little draws 47 curved ridge marks, then adds 26 more. How many ridge marks are in the drawing?
tasks.hint: Add the ones first. Regroup 13 ones as 1 ten and 3 ones.
tasks.worked: 47 + 26 = 73 ridge marks. Seven ones plus six ones makes 13, so regroup 10 ones as 1 ten.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: There are 68 paper pattern cards. Big puts away 29. How many cards remain on the table?
tasks.hint: Regroup 1 ten so 18 ones can take away 9 ones.
tasks.worked: 68 − 29 = 39 cards. Regroup 68 as 5 tens and 18 ones, then subtract.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: A tray holds 36 loop sketches and 58 whorl sketches. How many sketches are there altogether?
tasks.hint: Six ones plus eight ones makes 14 ones. Regroup 10 of them as 1 ten.
tasks.worked: 36 + 58 = 94 sketches. Regroup 14 ones as 1 ten and 4 ones, then add the tens.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: Little circles 46 details on a sheet with 72 ridge details. How many details are not circled?
tasks.hint: Regroup 1 ten so 12 ones can take away 6 ones.
tasks.worked: 72 − 46 = 26 details. Regroup 72 as 6 tens and 12 ones, then subtract.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Big sets out 59 cream print cards and 24 tan print cards. How many cards are ready?
tasks.hint: Nine ones plus four ones makes 13 ones. Regroup 10 ones as 1 ten.
tasks.worked: 59 + 24 = 83 cards. Regroup 13 ones as 1 ten and 3 ones, then add the tens.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: The field table begins with 81 magnifier cards and uses 37. How many magnifier cards are left?
tasks.hint: Regroup 1 ten so 11 ones can take away 7 ones.
tasks.worked: 81 − 37 = 44 cards. Regroup 81 as 7 tens and 11 ones, then subtract.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one equation and show the regrouping with tens and ones.
math.parentNote: Grade 2 math. Each problem uses two two-digit numbers and requires regrouping. The quantities belong to the paper story, not to measurements of real fingerprints.

writing.title: Describe a ridge map
writing.intro: Choose a close look and compare the paths you see.
writing.draw: Draw two large ridge paths. Add one ending and one split, then circle what changed.

frames.hint: tell where it ends or splits
connect a detail to your conclusion

writing.check: Did you name a detail and explain what that detail helped you notice?
writing.parentNote: Welcome speech, dictation, drawing, or writing. One careful comparison with evidence is enough.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Raised ridge tops touch the surface and leave lines; lower grooves do not touch, so they leave pale spaces.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Loop, whorl, and arch describe broad ridge flow. Ridge endings, splits, and other small details add a more specific map.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: The same turns, endings, and splits line up in both impressions even when pressure makes one lighter or smudged.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a spoken, dictated, drawn, or written comparison that names at least one visible ridge detail.

parentGuidance: This pack treats fingerprints as a pattern-and-printmaking study, not as an identity or crime activity. Keep any paper impressions at home; do not photograph, scan, upload, or share them. Use only a non-toxic washable stamp pad, press gently, and wash hands afterward. A fingerprint impression may be incomplete or smudged even though the friction-ridge arrangement beneath it is stable. Loop, whorl, and arch are broad pattern families; trained comparison uses smaller ridge details too.
